content: Hospital-acquired pneumonia is one of the most frequently encountered infections in hospitalized children worldwide. However, much of our current understanding of this condition in pediatric populations is extrapolated from studies conducted in adults. To date, no systematic review with meta-analysis has specifically evaluated the benefits and risks of various antibiotic regimens for treating hospital-acquired pneumonia in neonates and children. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of different antibiotic regimens for the treatment of hospital-acquired pneumonia in neonates and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and three additional databases, as well as two trial registries, up to February 2021. Additional studies were identified through reference checking, citation searching, and direct communication with study authors. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized clinical trials that compared one antibiotic regimen to another for the treatment of hospital-acquired pneumonia in neonates and children. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by three review authors. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The primary outcomes of interest were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events, while secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life, pneumonia-related mortality, non-serious adverse events, and treatment failure. The primary time point of interest was the maximum follow-up period reported in the studies. Four randomized clinical trials, involving a total of 84 participants, were included in the review. All four trials were assessed as having a high risk of bias. Due to the heterogeneity of the antibiotic regimens compared in these trials, no meta-analysis was conducted. Each trial evaluated a different antibiotic comparison: cefepime versus ceftazidime, linezolid versus vancomycin, meropenem versus cefotaxime, and ceftobiprole versus cephalosporin. Only one trial reported data on the primary outcomes of all-cause mortality and serious adverse events. Three trials provided data on the secondary outcome of treatment failure. However, two of these trials primarily included children with community-acquired pneumonia or other bacterial infections, meaning that children with hospital-acquired pneumonia represented only a subset of the study populations. The certainty of the evidence for all reported outcomes was deemed very low across all comparisons. As a result, no meaningful conclusions could be drawn from the numerical data provided. None of the included trials reported on health-related quality of life, pneumonia-related mortality, or non-serious adverse events. In conclusion, the available evidence is insufficient to determine the relative benefits and harms of different antibiotic regimens for hospital-acquired pneumonia in neonates and children. The very low certainty of the evidence precludes any recommendation of one antibiotic regimen over another. There is a clear need for well-designed randomized clinical trials to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of antibiotic treatments for this condition in pediatric populations.
